Why Halloween in User Acquisition peaked already in September
Tomas Hubka
Last updated: Oct 26, 2026
min read
Halloween ad volume in mobile games started three times earlier this year than it did two years ago, and the top-performing creatives aren’t new. For the ads at the top of the chart right now, Halloween is often one line of copy over gameplay that was already working. Here’s what the three-year trend looks like, why it’s happening, and what it means for your UA planning.
Halloween is this week, at least for regular mortals, but for user acquisition (UA) managers it’s already over. The seasonal creative window used to peak in late October, right when the holiday hit, however in recent years it has shifted closer to mid-September and has been winding down from there ever since. The pattern is bigger than one year, bigger than one studio, and it has implications for every seasonal moment on the calendar. Christmas and Valentine’s are next.
This piece looks at the three-year trend in Halloween creative volume, the two forces most likely driving the shift, and what the top-performing Halloween ads of this October actually look like when you examine them closely. The data comes from Ad Insights.
Three years, same pattern, bigger each time
Muhammad Asad Sohail already pulled the data on this year’s Halloween shift:
Muhammad compared 2025 and 2026, and I extended the view to three years. The shape remains the same: Each year, more Halloween ads show up earlier. The September 14 numbers tell the story most clearly. In 2024, around 570 new Halloween ads were live by mid-September. In 2025, that number tripled to roughly 1,670. In 2026, it jumped again to over 5,000. By October 31, which used to be the peak, the 2026 number has already settled below where it was two weeks earlier. The Halloween season isn’t ending later. It’s starting earlier and plateauing sooner.
New Halloween ads across three years, by two-week window. By mid-period in 2026, the volume of newly added Halloween ads had already surpassed what 2024 and 2025 reached at their late-October peaks, and continues to grow.
So why is this happening?
The simplest explanation is attention arbitrage. If everyone ships Halloween ads in late October, nobody wins. Networks saturate, CPMs climb, and your creative competes against hundreds of near-identical seasonal pitches. The teams going in early capture attention while the signal-to-noise ratio is still high. So while being first isn’t a competitive advantage, not being last surely is.
The second explanation is creative economics, though not the version you might expect. The obvious framing is that creative matters: a
2026 analysis of mobile UA strategy
estimates it accounts for roughly 56% of what drives incremental app installs. If that’s true, you’d expect every studio to be producing fresh seasonal creative for every seasonal moment. They aren’t, which points to a different conclusion.
To understand why, we should look at how UA economics have shifted over the last few years. Post-ATT and post-Privacy Sandbox, targeting precision has collapsed, and the then-traditional targeting signals UA teams used to rely on (device IDs, deterministic attribution, granular audience lookalikes) are either gone or heavily degraded. What’s left is creative as the main lever a team can pull. If you can’t target the right user, the creative itself has to do more of the work: catching the right eye, filtering for the right intent, converting the right install.
A bespoke seasonal creative that costs five figures to produce and runs for two weeks has to carry its own production cost plus the opportunity cost of the proven creative it displaces. A creative that’s been running for 300 days, by contrast, has a known conversion rate, known CPI, known fatigue curve, and known profit margin. Every day it runs is a day of extracted value from a sunk production cost. Replacing it with something new, even something seasonally themed, is a bet against evidence.
